notes: 39/39 tests, 69/69 assertions, port:parity --complete clean. All five jsdom stubs deleted. GAINED is the thesis: real layout + real ResizeObserver cover shared/useSize.ts L19-48, SliderThumbImpl.vue L40 (getThumbInBoundsOffset only runs once the thumb has a measured size) and Slider/utils.ts L67-70,L110-111. The single LOST line is itself a finding — see #linear-scale-degenerate. Two structural deviations, both recorded below: #form-submit-button and #home-end-name.

QUARANTINED via it.fails — reported, not fixed. The jsdom axe test is vacuous: Slider.test.ts:27-33 calls axe(wrapper.element) synchronously after mount(), before Vue flushes, so the thumb still carries display:none from SliderThumbImpl.vue:80 (the SSR anti-jank branch, active while value === undefined). axe skips hidden elements, so aria-input-field-name comes back INAPPLICABLE and the only interactive element in the component is never audited. await render() flushes, axe sees the thumb, and reports a real violation: single-thumb sliders have no accessible name because getLabel (utils.ts:35) only auto-labels 2+ thumbs and the story fixture supplies none. The gap is in the fixture, not the library. Not strictly a jsdom-vs-browser difference — jsdom reports it too once flushed (verified experimentally) — but browser mode is what surfaced it. Resolve by giving _Slider.vue an aria-label, NOT by disabling the rule.

The only line the browser port fails to cover is Slider/utils.ts:109 — linearScale's `if (input[0] === input[1]) return output[0]` short-circuit. jsdom takes that branch on EVERY pointer test, because the slider measures 0x0 so `rect.width - thumbWidth` is 0; the browser takes L110-111, the real interpolation, instead. So a line the jsdom suite reports as covered was only ever covered by the absence of layout, and the arithmetic the component actually ships was never executed. This is the coverage-parity oracle's first justified LOST line; exempted via PORT-COVERAGE-ALLOW.tsv, which is machine-checked against this file. Generalises: coverage lost to a port is not automatically a regression, but it must be argued line by line.

The jsdom form block fires a synthetic `submit` on the <form>, which no user can do. Ported with a real <button type="submit"> (see AGENTS.md 'Settled questions' — implicit submission via Enter on the focused thumb does NOT submit this form, 0 calls, and neither suite would have caught that). Also: vitest-browser-vue unmounts after every test, so the component is rendered per test in a beforeEach rather than once at describe-body level as the original does. The module-level handleSubmit spy still accumulates calls across tests, so the original's 1-then-2 call-count assertions port unchanged.

Naming bug in the jsdom original, carried over verbatim: under 'when vertical > when inverted', `it('home should set value to 100')` asserts 0 and `it('end should set value to 0')` asserts 100. The assertions are right — Home/End are semantic (min/max) per ARIA APG and ignore `inverted` by design — and the names are simply wrong. PORTING.md rule 4 says to fix the test so the name becomes true, but applying it here would fail a component that is behaving correctly, so the assertions were kept and the deviation recorded here. Browser mode contributed nothing to finding this; reading the file did.

MUTATION-VERIFIED (PORTING.md 2.3), the T3 thesis proved rather than asserted. Deleting `target.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId)` from SliderImpl.vue's pointerdown handler — i.e. breaking pointer capture outright — makes the browser port's 'should emit valueCommit on wrapper' FAIL and leaves the jsdom test PASSING. jsdom passes because its own mock, `hasPointerCapture: vi.fn().mockImplementation(id => id)`, answers yes for a capture that was never taken, so pointerup still emits slideEnd. The jsdom test cannot fail this mutation by construction. Source reverted immediately; verified with git diff.

PORTED, 10/10 tests and 18/18 assertions; port:parity --complete and port:checklist --complete both clean; coverage loses nothing. VERDICT REVISED — this row previously read `stay-jsdom` and recommended skipping the other 12 T1 files. That recommendation is withdrawn: the goal is to remove jsdom from the repo entirely, so "the port gains nothing" is no longer a reason not to port, and only files needing NO DOM (which go to the `node` project) are exempt. This one mounts components, so it is DOM-dependent and belongs in browser mode regardless of what it gains. THE MEASUREMENTS STAND and are still the honest cost of the tier: steady state over 3 runs each, total wall clock 1.11s jsdom vs 1.72s browser (1.5x), vitest Duration 539ms vs 1.17s (2.2x), test execution 17ms vs 45ms (2.7x). The useful half is the absolute number — a cold Chromium launch cost ~0.6s, so browser mode is not the multi-second tax the tiering assumed, which is exactly why an all-browser end state is affordable. Note the port deleted no stubs, because a file that mocks nothing has nothing to delete; the value here is jsdom removal, not mock removal. Single gained coverage line is not a browser win, see #auto-unmount.

GENERALISES TO ALL 97 FILES, AND IS A TRAP IN THE ORACLE. The one line the browser port covers and jsdom does not is useForwardExpose.ts:68 — the `if (!ref) return` detach path, which Vue runs only when a template ref is released at unmount. Chromium has nothing to do with it: vitest-browser-vue registers beforeEach(cleanup), and cleanup() calls wrapper.unmount() (dist/index.js + dist/pure-*.js), so every ported test tears its component down, whereas the jsdom original mounts 10 times and never unmounts once. Verified, not assumed: a throwaway jsdom test doing mount() then wrapper.unmount() covers L68 with istanbul hit count 1 (probe written, measured, deleted). Two lessons. (1) A coverage GAIN from port:coverage is not automatically evidence for browser mode — check whether the harness or the environment earned it, or the thesis gets credited with wins it did not achieve. (2) The more useful direction: reka-ui jsdom suite exercises almost no component teardown, and porting picks that up for free.

AUDIT OF THE OTHER 12 T1 FILES. CONCLUSION REVISED — this row previously concluded `stay-jsdom` for all 12. Under the delete-jsdom goal the split is different: 4 of the 12 need no DOM at all and have MOVED TO THE `node` PROJECT (date/calendar, shared/color/gradient, shared/color/utils, shared/useSingleOrMultipleValue), and the remaining 8 are DOM-dependent and are queued for browser mode (component/Arrow, getActiveElement, useArrowNavigation, useComposing, useForwardProps, useForwardScopeId, useIsUsingKeyboard, useSelectionBehavior). THE EVIDENCE THE AUDIT PRODUCED IS UNCHANGED AND STILL WORTH HAVING, because it says these 8 ports should be expected to be boring rather than revealing: each of the 4 non-pure files was checked against the specific way its jsdom test could be green for the wrong reason, and all 4 came back negative. The notable one is getActiveElement, an expected WIN that was not one — the function is nothing but a shadow-DOM retargeting loop, so a jsdom that failed to retarget would make that loop dead code (the Slider-axe failure mode). Probed both environments on the test own nested-shadow fixture: identical. document.activeElement is the OUTER HOST and the loop iterates exactly 2 times in jsdom and Chromium alike. jsdom shadow-DOM focus retargeting is faithful. Also negative: useIsUsingKeyboard (6 lines of listener registration, no isTrusted check, so synthetic events hit the identical path), useArrowNavigation (pure function over querySelectorAll; its one focus() call acts on detached elements neither environment verifies), component/Arrow (single axe test over a decorative <svg> with no text or interactive content, so the rules that come alive in Chromium have nothing to apply to). Port them for jsdom removal, not for findings.

TEN FILES NEVER NEEDED JSDOM AND NO LONGER USE IT — the first jsdom deletions in the repo, and the cheapest ones available. Under the delete-jsdom goal the question per file stopped being "does browser mode add value" and became "does this file touch the DOM at all". Scanned all 97 jsdom files for DOM signals (@vue/test-utils, @testing-library, vitest-axe, document/window/HTMLElement, DOM event constructors, navigator) and got 87 that do and 10 that do not: Drawer/utils, Splitter/utils/{callPanelCallbacks,units,validation}, date/calendar, index, shared/color/{gradient,utils}, shared/useNonce, shared/useSingleOrMultipleValue. Verified by running them, not just by grepping: a third vitest project (`node`, environment node, NO setup file) runs all 10 green — 571 tests, 28% of the whole suite. They needed neither jsdom nor a browser, and they load none of vitest.setup.ts jsdom patches (canvas mock, jest-dom matchers, getComputedStyle fix). Cost side, same 10 files: jsdom spends 2.71s in setup files and 2.92s in environment construction (cumulative across workers) where node spends 0ms and 2ms. Note shared/useNonce is tagged T4-hostile for its vi.mock, which turns out to be irrelevant — module mocking works fine in a node environment. Project split now: node 10 files/571 tests, unit(jsdom) 87/1444, browser 4/51. The migration is done when `unit` matches nothing.

THE T2 TRIAL RUN (PORTING.md phase 1). 7/7 tests, 7/7 assertions, port:parity --complete and port:checklist --complete clean, coverage gains 1 line and loses none. Mechanically the easiest port so far and still worth three further findings, which is the argument for running T2 as real ports rather than assuming they are rubber-stamps. Two translation gaps the table did not cover, both now added to AGENTS.md. (1) The original uses @testing-library/vue render, not VTU mount, and asserts on .html() four times; vitest-browser-vue exposes no VTU wrapper and therefore no .html() at all (its render returns container / locator / emitted / rerender / unmount and the locator selectors). @testing-library/vue's is literally "html: () => wrapper.html()" (dist/render.js:53), i.e. the component root's outerHTML, so container.firstElementChild.outerHTML is the exact translation and all four expected strings port unchanged. A locator assertion is NOT a substitute here: the original pins the ENTIRE rendered output, and toHaveAttribute would check one attribute and let extra ones through. (2) The original's beforeEach clearing document.body.innerHTML is deleted outright — render unmounts and removes its container after every test. AXE IS NOT VACUOUS HERE, unlike Slider's: probed the result object, 5 rules pass (label, form-field-multiple-labels, label-title-only, duplicate-id-aria, color-contrast), so await render flushed and axe audited the real thing. color-contrast is the notable one — it is inert under jsdom and live in Chromium, so the port audits one rule more than the original could.

THE JSDOM TEST CLICKS AN ELEMENT NO USER COULD HIT. Both click tests in the original render a bare h(Label) with no slot, then call container.getElementsByTagName('label')[0].click(). An empty <label> is an inline box with no content: MEASURED at 0x18 in Chromium — zero WIDTH, full line-height — and Playwright refuses to click a zero-size element, so locator.click() retries and times out (probed with an explicit 1500ms timeout). jsdom does not care, because HTMLElement.click() dispatches on any node regardless of layout, and jsdom has no layout to consult. The port therefore gives both labels a text slot the original does not have. That is a deviation from the original body, recorded here rather than buried: it is forced by the environment, it cannot affect what is under test (the input is a SIBLING, not nested, so label text cannot create an implicit association), and it makes the test describe a gesture a user can actually perform. THE ASSERTIONS ARE UNCHANGED AND ARE NOT VACUOUS — verified by probing the positive case: the same real click on a label whose "for" DOES match focuses the input, so these two tests discriminate rather than passing because nothing happened. GENERALISES: any jsdom test that clicks an element with no intrinsic size is asserting about a gesture that cannot occur, and browser mode turns that from a silent pass into a timeout.

THE GAINED LINE, AND THE ENVIRONMENT EARNED IT — checked per PORTING.md 2.2 rather than assumed. The one line the port covers and jsdom does not is Label.vue:24, the inline @mousedown handler, which is the component's ONLY behaviour beyond rendering a <label> (it prevents text selection on double click). HTMLElement.click() — what the original calls, and what VTU's trigger('click') does too — dispatches a click event and NOTHING ELSE: no pointerdown, no mousedown, no focus, no mouseup. A real Playwright click dispatches the full sequence, so the handler runs. This is not a harness artifact of the kind #auto-unmount warns about: a jsdom test written this way cannot reach that line in ANY environment, and the coverage oracle proves it — the jsdom run performed the identical gesture on the identical element and reported the line uncovered. GENERALISES HARD, and is the best reason found so far to port T2 files that look boring: every mousedown / pointerdown / focus handler in the library is invisible to a jsdom test that clicks. BUT THE GAIN STOPS SHORT OF THE LOGIC, which line counts hide. Reading the istanbul BRANCH map instead: L24 carries two statements (hit 2 and 0) and its if-branch is [0,2] — taken zero times. event.detail > 1 is never true because no test in EITHER suite double-clicks, so preventDefault never runs and the double-click prevention this component exists to provide is exercised by nobody. A covered line is not a tested behaviour. Deliberately not fixed: adding that test would be an INVENTED it, which port:parity rejects and rule 7 forbids.

A GAP IN THE ORIGINAL SUITE, CARRIED OVER VERBATIM. Label has exactly one job — associate a <label> with a control via "for" — and the file tests it only in the negative: "should not focus the input when click on the label without a for attribute" and "...with a for attribute that does not match any input". Neither suite has a test that clicking a label whose "for" DOES match focuses the input, so both negatives would pass against a component that did nothing whatsoever. Confirmed live while validating the port (probe: real click on a matching label, document.activeElement becomes the INPUT), so the behaviour works and is simply unasserted. Left alone deliberately: a new it() is an INVENTED test that port:parity fails and rule 7 forbids, so the deliverable is this row rather than a patch. Worth noting the gap is not really the library's — "for" association is browser behaviour and this component only has to avoid breaking it — which is precisely the class of thing a jsdom suite cannot meaningfully assert and a browser suite can.
